The View from SomewherePart III · Surveys that overlap

Chapter 11

Contextuality by default

Web edition. Figure 11.4 is live: move the point, change the misreport or search for false alarms.

Go back to the renters of Chapter 8, with one change that is small and not far-fetched. Survey 1 asks the rent question X right after the car question Y. Survey 2 asks the same words, but right after the work-from-home question Z. Chapter 8 treated the two answers to X as two draws of one variable. That is what let it demand that the surveys agree on the share of renters, pool their tables when they nearly did, and blame any gap on sampling noise. Suppose that is false. Suppose that after the work question, a few more people in the whole city would say “I rent” than after the car question, and that no larger sample would make the gap go away. This is an invented scenario, but it is the situation survey methodologists worry about, and it is the situation physicists were in when they started asking the same question about particles.

There is then no single X to hand to both tables, and the loop test of Chapter 8 stops meaning what it meant. A rejection might say the three tables cannot come from one population. It might equally say that the same question was a different question in survey 2. This chapter is about telling those apart, or about finding out that you cannot. The summary, so you can read the rest with it in mind: a rule from physics and psychology, contextuality-by-default, treats the two answers as two variables and forgives margin gaps in a precisely defined way; the pooling rule of Chapter 10 treats them as one. We ran both on simulated surveys. They fail in opposite directions, and no test of the tables alone can say which failure you are in.

None of this is new. The split between margin gaps and failure to glue dates from 2015, and the chapter says where.

11.1One question, two variables

Label every answer by the survey that collected it. Write X1 for X as asked in survey 1 and X2 for X as asked in survey 2; likewise Y1, Y3, Z2, Z3. Each survey is a context, and it contains the variables that survey measured: survey 1: (X1,Y1),survey 2: (X2,Z2),survey 3: (Y3,Z3).survey 1: (X1,Y1),survey 2: (X2,Z2),survey 3: (Y3,Z3). Within a context we have a joint distribution, because the same people answered both questions: that is the two-by-two table. Across contexts we have nothing. No respondent appears in two surveys, so no person has both an X1 and an X2, and the data contain no joint distribution of the two. The pair (X1,X2) is the copy of one question in two contexts, and a set of copies of one question is called a connection. Figure 11.1 draws the whole system. It is a ring of six variables, with solid edges where a table exists and dashed edges where two copies share a name and nothing else.

When all copies of a question have the same distribution the system is called consistently connected. It goes by other names, no-signaling in physics and marginal selectivity outside it among them. It is the situation of Chapter 8, where the shared margin was one number and sampling noise was the only reason two surveys could disagree about it. When some copies have different distributions the system is inconsistently connected, and that is the case here. The difference between two copies’ distributions is called a direct influence of the context on the answer: asking after the work question moved the rent answers directly.

The point of splitting X into X1 and X2 is that the question “is there a joint distribution?” becomes cheap to answer and therefore uninformative. A joint of all six variables with the right tables always exists, because we are free to tie the copies together however we like; make them independent if nothing better comes to mind. What carries information is how tightly the copies must be tied. Chapter 8 tied them to be equal, which is possible only when their margins agree. Contextuality-by-default ties them as tightly as their margins allow.

11.2Tied as tightly as the margins allow

Take two copies of one yes-or-no question, with P(X1=1)=p and P(X2=1)=q. A coupling is any joint distribution of the pair with these margins. How often can the copies agree? The cell where both are 0 holds at most min(1−p,1−q) of the mass and the cell where both are 1 at most min(p,q), so P(X1=X2)≤min(1−p,1−q)+min(p,q)=1−|p−q|. The bound is reached. Put all the mass the margins permit on the diagonal and let the leftover mass, exactly |p−q| of it, sit in the one off-diagonal cell that the margins demand. That is the maximal coupling (Figure 11.2). It is unique for two-valued variables. Its disagreement mass is the total-variation distance between the two margins, which is the least change in answers that turns one distribution into the other.

When the margins are equal, the maximal coupling makes the copies identical, and contextuality-by-default reduces to the gluing question of Chapter 8. When they differ, the rule says: the copies disagree by exactly the margin gap, which is attributed to the context’s direct influence, and nothing more. The system is called noncontextual if some joint distribution of all six variables has the right tables and couples every pair of copies maximally. Otherwise it is contextual. Margin gaps by themselves never make a system contextual. Only a failure that remains once every connection has been tied as tightly as it can be does.

This is a rule, and its authors say plainly that it is one choice among others: any other constraint on how copies may be coupled defines another notion of noncontextuality. I come back to that in Section 11.6, because it is where the econometrics lives.

11.3The criterion for a loop of three

For a ring of n two-valued questions, Kujala, Dzhafarov and Larsson give a necessary and sufficient condition for noncontextuality. Code the answers ±1, with yes as −1. For the ring of Figure 11.1 (n=3) the data are three correlations, EXY,EXZ,EYZ, one per survey, and three margin gaps, one per connection: δX=|EX1−EX2|,δY=|EY1−EY3|,δZ=|EZ2−EZ3|.δX=|EX1−EX2|,δY=|EY1−EY3|,δZ=|EZ2−EZ3|. In this chapter’s notation, the system is noncontextual exactly when maxodd # of minus signs(±EXY±EXZ±EYZ±(1−δX)±(1−δY)±(1−δZ))≤4, the maximum running over sign choices with an odd number of minus signs. Call the left side minus 4 the number Δ, so Δ>0 means contextual. The paper’s general statement is for n questions with the bound 2n−2, and for n=3,4,5 with consistent margins it becomes the Leggett–Garg, CHSH and KCBS inequalities of physics. We took this form from our notes on the main text and coded it; the form of the margin terms is checked below, not quoted.

Two readings help. First, with equal margins every δ is zero, the margin terms contribute 3, and the condition is a triangle inequality on the three correlations. In Chapter 8’s units it is d≤a+b and its three siblings: the faces of the tetrahedron. Here the term for the face d=a+b is EXY+EXZ−EYZ−1=2(d−a−b).

Second, the margin gaps enter linearly and with a minus sign. In every set of tables we tried, Δ has the same sign as [maxodd(±EXY±EXZ±EYZ)−1]−(δX+δY+δZ), the loop violation of the correlations less the total margin gap. This is not ours: the paper states it as its inequality (5), builds its confidence interval on it, and notes in a footnote that it is equivalent to the criterion, citing a proof by Kujala and Dzhafarov that we have not read. We checked it anyway. We drew 1,500 random sets of three tables, each table from a different random population so that margins differ, and the two signs agreed every time (the script is figures/ch11_numbers.py). The same script confirms Δ against a linear program that searches directly for the best coupling over all 26 joint outcomes of the six variables: the verdicts agree on all 1,500 sets, and on the 28 contextual ones the best coupling falls short of the agreement the margins allow by exactly Δ/2. In words: every unit of margin gap buys one unit of forgiveness for the loop. Everything in the next two sections is that sentence, seen from different angles.

11.4Two rules, one misreport

We set up the experiment of research cycle 7 and look at it first with exact tables, no sampling. The design is Chapter 8’s with a=b=0.2 and every question answered yes half the time, so a single population exists exactly when d≤0.4. Survey 2 misreports X: a respondent whose true X is 0 reports 1 with probability s, whatever the respondent’s Z. Surveys 1 and 3 are correct. So the reported tables are survey 1 and survey 3 as before and a survey 2 whose X margin has moved. The truth, a coherent population for d≤0.4 and none for d>0.4, does not depend on s.

Two methods read the reported tables:

  • By default: compute Δ as in Section 11.3.

  • Pooling: Chapter 10’s rule. Reconcile the margins by projecting the twelve numbers onto the span of tables that one joint could produce, then ask whether the projected point lies in the cone of nonnegative joints. A positive squared distance from the cone is called “outside”.

The misreport moves two things in Δ. The X margin gap is s in ±1 coding, because half the population has true X=0 and a share s of them change to 1, which moves the mean of the ±1 variable by 2⋅12s. And the reported correlation drops. The misreport turns X=+1 into −1 for a share s/2 of respondents, which lowers E[XZ] by 2sE[Z1{X=+1}]=s(EZ+E[XZ])=0.6s, since EZ=0 and E[XZ]=0.6; so EXZ=0.6(1−s). Put them in the face that binds for d>0.4: Δ=EXY+EXZ−EYZ−1−δX=0.6+0.6(1−s)−(1−2d)−1−s=2d−0.8−1.6s. This is our algebra for this one design; it matches the exact tables of experiment 7 at all twenty of its points with d≥0.4 (for instance d=0.5, s=0.1 gives 0.04, and d=0.6, s=0.2 gives 0.08). So by default forgives incoherence at 1.6 per unit of s, and at d=0.5 calls the system noncontextual once s≥0.125. Figure 11.3 shows the surface.

Pooling is forgiving too, but more slowly. Scanning s from 0 to 0.6 at each d from 0.40 to 0.60 (the same script), the pooled point leaves the outside of the cone along what reads as the line s=(d−0.4)/0.3. At d=0.5 that is s=1/3, against 0.125 by default; the memo’s coarser grid says only “near 0.4”, which is consistent. Figure 11.4 puts the two boundaries on one map.

Look at what Figure 11.4 shows about errors. For a system that is really incoherent, the by-default rule is the one that misses: it forgives, in proportion to the margin gap, something the margin gap did not cause. Pooling is the more sensitive of the two. On this map neither method raises a false alarm on a coherent system. Our first grid for cycle 7 looked exactly like this and missed something: pooling can be pushed into a false alarm. Even this design does it at smaller d than the map shows: for d≤0.2 pooling says “incoherent” once s>d/0.3, by the same script, while by default stays silent. Section 11.8 shows where else.

11.5When a misreport meets a second variable

Cycle 7’s misreport ignored everyone’s Z. That made it a very special change, and the by-default rule is exactly right for it by construction. The misreport changes the answers of a share s/2 of respondents and moves the margin by that same amount, so the changed answers and the margin gap are the same quantity. Copies tied together this way are maximally coupled. The rule cannot be fooled by a misreport that looks like its own definition of a context effect.

Cycle 8 asks what happens when the misreport depends on the respondent’s Z. One population exists behind the true answers throughout, so any verdict of “incoherent” is a false alarm. Survey 2’s report of X is changed in one of three ways, drawn in Figure 11.5 on the (X,Z) table:

  • assimilate: if the true X differs from Z, report X=Z with probability s;

  • contrast: if the true X equals Z, report X≠Z with probability s;

  • one-sided: if Z=1 and the true X is 0, report 1 with probability s.

In the symmetric design, assimilation does something instructive. Its two flows have equal size, so P(X=1) in survey 2 does not move at all. Every margin gap is zero and by default has nothing to forgive. But the flows take mass from the disagreeing cells to the agreeing ones, so survey 2’s disagreement rate falls from b to b(1−s). With d=0.38, inside the band, and s=0.4, survey 2 reports a disagreement of 0.12 rather than 0.2, and the third survey’s d=0.38 now exceeds a+b′=0.2+0.12=0.32. The triangle inequality fails with no margin gap to absorb it, and Δ=2(0.38−0.32)=0.12. That is exactly the exact-table value of experiment 8. A population exists and every method rejects it. Contrast does the mirror thing.

The one-sided misreport behaves differently, and the reason is a general fact about two-valued variables. Suppose answers move only from 0 to 1, with any dependence on anything else. The share of respondents whose answer changes is then the same as the increase in the share answering 1, which is the margin gap. Changed answers and margin gap are the same quantity, so the pairs of copies are maximally coupled again and by default stays silent. A misreport that runs in both directions changes more answers than the net margin shift records, and the excess can show up as incoherence the margins cannot excuse. (This is a statement about two values. With three or more, “one direction” is not enough, and Chapter 13 is about what replaces it.)

11.6What the data cannot say

Put the two sections together and a pattern appears. In cycle 7, a real margin shift hid real incoherence from the by-default rule. In cycle 8, an effect that moved no margin at all produced incoherence out of a coherent population. Both are one fact seen from the two sides: a difference in how a shared question is measured and a failure of the tables to cohere trade off against each other, and the tables alone cannot say which you have.

Take the symmetric assimilation case again. Survey 2 reports disagreement 0.12 where truth is 0.2. Those three tables are also exactly what you would see in a city where renters and home workers truly differ 12 percent of the time, the other pairs are as reported, and the triangle fails for real. The two stories differ only in what they assume about how X is measured in survey 2. The first assumes a particular rule linking survey 2’s X to the X of survey 1 (assimilation); the second assumes the rule is the identity. That assumed rule is not estimable from these data, because no respondent appears in two surveys. The same holds for the cycle 7 case: d=0.5 with s=0.2 is called noncontextual by the by-default criterion, which on its own terms is not an error, because a joint with maximal couplings exists. The data cannot distinguish two different populations from one population plus a suitably correlated misreport.

This is what we take the identification point to be, and it is the place where this project’s old idea of frames reappears in probability language. In Chapter 1 a restriction map that is not the identity let two local views keep different frames, and Chapter 4 followed what happens when such maps do not compose around a loop. Here the rule that couples the copies of X plays the role of the restriction map. Maximal coupling is one such rule, equality is another, and different rules give different loop tests. The authors of the by-default theory say as much about maximal coupling; I come back to the paper below. We have not checked whether anyone has written down the correspondence between contextuality-by-default and sheaves with non-identity restriction maps. It may exist.

What a loop test on survey tables rejects, then, is a joint hypothesis: one population, and the shared questions measured the same way in every survey (under pooling), or one population, and the shared questions related by maximal coupling (by default). The simple recipe that cycle 7 suggested was to test the margins first, pool and test the loop if they agree, and read the by-default verdict as the conservative one if they do not. The symmetric assimilation case is the hole in it: the margins agree, so the recipe says pool and trust a rejection, and the rejection is wrong.

11.7What the papers say

What the paper says: Kujala, Dzhafarov and Larsson (2015), “Necessary and sufficient conditions for an extended noncontextuality in a broad class of quantum mechanical systems”

We read the main text in full and not the supplementary proofs. The paper labels every measurement by its context, so that the same property in two contexts is two random variables; it calls the set of copies a connection, and it lists many names for consistent connectedness. For inconsistently connected systems it asks for a joint in which each connection’s copies agree as often as their margins allow, and for a cycle of n two-valued properties it proves a necessary and sufficient inequality, which reduces to the Leggett–Garg, CHSH and KCBS inequalities when margins are consistent. Its inference is a conservative interval (a Bonferroni construction) on the margin-gap form of Section 11.3. It says nothing about econometric inequality testing. That is a gap the paper does not claim to fill, and Chapters 15 and 16 are about it.

What the paper says: Dzhafarov and Kujala (2016), “Context-content systems of random variables: the contextuality-by-default theory”

We read only the conclusion, so what follows is limited to what the conclusion says. The authors insist that inconsistency of connectedness be kept apart from contextuality. They note that whether a system is contextual depends on how one sorts variables into contents and contexts, a sorting made before the theory is applied. They note that maximal coupling is one choice of constraint among many, and that any constraint defines its own noncontextuality. And they state how their setting differs from Abramsky’s (Chapter 9): because variables in different contexts are different variables, the problem is not posed as the compatibility of overlapping groups of random variables. The definitions we use in this chapter come from the 2015 paper above and not from this one.

What the paper says: Dzhafarov, Zhang and Kujala (2016), “Is there contextuality in behavioral and social systems?”

We read the abstract and the conclusion only. They review polls, visual illusions, conjoint choices, word combinations and psychophysical matching, and report that none of these data gives evidence of contextuality. Their working hypothesis is that in behavioral and social systems every context effect is a direct influence, that is, a margin shift, and never a failure of the copies to be coupled. That is a claim about the data they reviewed, under their definition. It is not a claim that surveys are free of the effects of Sections 11.4 and 11.5: a two-way effect on an association can be, by their definition, a contextuality, and the working hypothesis says they did not find one. We did not read the body of the paper, and we did not look for later challenges to it; Chapter 17 reads a later paper from the same group that reports a case of contextuality in a psychophysical experiment. For this project the review is an empirical prior: it says that in human data the action may be in the margins, and the loop obstruction may be close to zero.

11.8What we found

Cycle 6: the split is prior art. Experiment 5 of Chapter 10 had split the test statistic into a part that measures disagreeing margins and a part that measures failure to glue after pooling, and we had counted that split as an improvement on the test. Kujala, Dzhafarov and Larsson drew a version of the same distinction in 2015. The two differ in what they assume about the shared questions:

By default Pooling
A shared question is two variables one variable seen twice
Margin disagreement is real sampling noise
Treatment couple the copies maximally project by least squares

We compared the two on simulated surveys with truly equal margins, a=b=0.2 and 1,000 replications. The population value of Δ is −0.4,0,0.1,0.2 at d=0.2,0.4,0.45,0.5. Sample verdicts, where “contextual” means Δ^>0 and “outside” means a positive loop distance:

Third survey n Both Pooling only By default only Mean Δ^ (true)
d=0.4 500 0.046 0.425 0.000 −0.15 (0)
d=0.45 500 0.284 0.636 0.000 −0.05 (0.10)
d=0.5 500 0.700 0.296 0.000 0.05 (0.20)
d=0.45 2000 0.703 0.296 0.000 0.02 (0.10)
d=0.5 2000 0.991 0.009 0.000 0.13 (0.20)

By default never called a sample contextual that pooling had put inside the cone. Two things in the table are worth reading closely. The plug-in Δ^ is biased toward “noncontextual”, by about 0.15 at n=500 and 0.08 at n=2000, because it subtracts the absolute margin gaps and sampling noise makes those positive even when the true margins are equal: noise is charged as direct influence. The bias is elementary, the expected absolute value of a mean-zero normal, and surely known to the people who use the method. We did not look for where. And the comparison was unfair to by default in one direction: we generated the data with equal margins, which is pooling’s own assumption. A crude bootstrap test on Δ^ (reject when its fifth percentile is positive; the rule is ours and is not bias-corrected) rejected 0.7 percent of the time at d=0.5, n=500 and 55 percent at n=2000, against 93 and 100 percent for the loop part of Chapter 10.

Cycle 7: margins that really differ. Now the design of Section 11.4, at n=2000 per survey, 400 replications, a five percent level, and for by-default a bootstrap lower bound on Δ with the bias corrected. (The correction raised the rejection rate at d=0.5, s=0 from 0.55 to 0.90.) The columns are rejection rates of the test that the shared margins agree, of the test on the loop part, and of the by-default test.

Truth s Margins Loop part By default
one population, d=0.2 0 0.055 0.000 0.000
one population, d=0.2 0.1 0.743 0.000 0.000
one population, d=0.38 0.1 0.773 0.000 0.000
one population, d=0.38 0.2 1.000 0.000 0.000
none, d=0.5 0 0.045 1.000 0.903
none, d=0.5 0.1 0.765 0.990 0.103
none, d=0.5 0.2 1.000 0.730 0.000
none, d=0.6 0.2 1.000 1.000 0.303

Read down the last four rows. At d=0.5 and s=0.1 the pooled loop test rejects 99 percent of the time and by default 10. The margin test, which asks only whether the shared margins agree, catches a misreport of 0.1 about three times in four and one of 0.2 every time. The coherent populations in this table raised no false alarm. Our first grid missed pooling’s weakness completely, because it appears when the population sits near a face of the cone that the misreport pushes it across, and our grid never put it there: its populations near a face, d=0.38 and 0.4, were pushed away from it. When the grid showed nothing, we searched for a false alarm. We drew 5,000 random populations per cell, from a Dirichlet distribution on the eight answer strings, with all parameters equal to 1 for “diffuse” and 0.2 for “concentrated”, let survey 2 misreport X in a random direction, and counted verdicts of “incoherent” on exact tables:

Random populations s Pooled point outside cone By default contextual
Diffuse 0.05 0.2% 0
Diffuse 0.2 2.1% 0
Diffuse 0.4 8.5% 0
Concentrated 0.05 34.9% 0
Concentrated 0.2 54.7% 0
Concentrated 0.4 65.7% 0

By default raised no false alarm in 40,000 draws (eight cells; the two at s=0.1 are not shown), which is what theory predicts when the misreport is a maximal coupling. Pooling raised many, because a concentrated population has most of its mass on a few answer strings, sits near a face of the cone, and is easily pushed across it. Two limits belong with this table. These are exact tables, with no sampling, and the search counts any positive distance, so many of the concentrated-population alarms would be too small to reject in a sample. We did not simulate that. And it is one misreport, the one under which by default is right by construction. The conclusion we drew is a comparison and not a ranking: pooling and the by-default criterion err in opposite directions. By default forgives real incoherence in proportion to the margin gap; pooling declares coherent populations incoherent when a survey misreports.

Cycle 8: a misreport that depends on Z. The same experiment with the three mechanisms of Section 11.5, 5,000 random populations per cell, exact tables, share called incoherent:

Every by-default false alarm was also a pooling false alarm. The one-sided mechanism raised none in 20,000 populations (its s=0.1 cells are not shown), even though it depends on Z, for the reason given in Section 11.5. In a later addendum we ran a fourth mechanism, one where mass moves within a diagonal of the (X,Z) table, so that agreement is unchanged and both margins move: by default raised no false alarm in all twelve cells (60,000 populations), and pooling up to 55 percent. Where that mechanism comes from is the subject of Chapter 12.

In the structured symmetric case, with samples of 2,000 per survey and 400 replications (same three columns):

Case Margins Loop part By default
d=0.38, assimilate 0.2 0.063 0.323 0.073
d=0.38, assimilate 0.4 0.053 0.988 0.473
d=0.38, one-sided 0.4 0.535 0.345 0.005
d=0.2, contrast 0.4 0.053 1.000 0.950

In the second row, the margin test has power equal to its size, the loop test rejects 99 percent and by default 47: a coherent population measured with a symmetric context effect is indistinguishable from no population. That is the identification point in numbers, and it is the hole in cycle 7’s recipe. The mechanism tables need one more caveat: one-way safety is a fact about two-valued variables. With three values, cycle 9 found it false (Chapter 13).

Two cautions about the whole chapter. Everything here is the smallest design: binary variables, three surveys, identity weighting, one misreport at a time. And the mapping from the effects survey methodologists report onto our three mechanisms is ours, which Chapter 12 examines.
